Topic T1 · First Impression

What You’d Notice Picking This Up Cold

Item H2 is a small, smooth steel pin with no head and no thread. Three things stand out before you ever read the print: the plain ground body, the chamfered ends, and the bright zinc finish.

As received: plain cylindrical body, chamfered ends and a bright zinc finish (reference photo from the SBS item page).
The same geometry in the SBS 3D CAD model: a plain cylinder, no head, chamfered end.

No Head, No Drive — A dowel pin has no head. It doesn’t clamp; it locates two parts precisely against each other.

Plain Ground Body — Constant 4 mm diameter, ground smooth and burr-free (geschliffen, gratfrei on the print). No thread.

Zinc (Cr3) Finish — The bright, slightly blue-silver surface is electroplated zinc with a trivalent chromate passivate.

Chamfered Ends — Both ends are chamfered and rounded (the print shows 15° and a radius), so the pin starts easily into its hole.

The DIN 6325 Standard Itself
Click the image to enlarge.
DIN 6325, October 1971: Zylinderstifte, gehärtet, Toleranzfeld m6 — parallel pins, hardened, tolerance zone m6. Read the full DIN 6325 standard ↗
  1. The d = 4 column — the 4 mm pin: end geometry of l2 = 1, r ≈ 4, z1 ≈ 0.6 and z2 ≈ 0.4 mm, plus one weight per available length.
  2. The 28 mm row — where it crosses the 4 mm column (red box): 2.76 kg per 1,000 pieces, about 2.8 g each. The item page rounds this to 0.01 lbs per EA.
  3. Werkstoff / Ausführung — material and condition: steel with a tensile strength of at least 600 N/mm², hardened, 60 ± 2 HRC.

A 1971 Standard, Still on the Drawing

DIN 6325 dates from October 1971, and the Standards Library lists it as Active alongside ISO 8734 (1997), each as the other’s alternate. Check which one a print calls out: the library summary quotes a hardness of 550–650 HV30, while the 1971 DIN page itself prints 60 ± 2 HRC, the figure this module uses. The page says its pins are used mainly as locating pins for tools, jigs and gauges (Paßstifte für Werkzeuge, Spannzeuge und Meßzeuge).

Topic T4 · Material Selection

Hardened Steel, 60 ± 2 HRC

Unlike a stainless screw, a dowel pin has no material letter in its part number. The standard does the talking: what the steel is, and how hard it must be.

Requirement

Material: steel, tensile strength of at least 600 N/mm² · Condition: hardened, 60 ± 2 HRC (DIN 6325)

What “HRC” Means

Rockwell C, a hardness scale for hardened steel. 60 HRC is very hard — roughly 700 on the Vickers scale, in the range of cutting tools and files.Most screws sit far lower: a typical alloy-steel cap screw is in the range of 32–44 HRC.

Why Harden a Dowel?

A dowel is driven into a hole and has to stay exactly where it is. A hard surface resists denting, wear and shear, so the pin keeps its size and its position through repeated use.

The Trade-Off

Hard steel has little ductility. A hardened pin is meant to be loaded in shear, side to side, and not bent or struck. It is a locator, not a bolt.

Grade Reads “Steel”

The standard sets performance (strength and hardness), not an alloy. That is why the Grade field on the item page says simply Steel, and why hardness is the number to remember.

Why It Matters

At 60 HRC the finish is not just cosmetic. Plating a part this hard raises questions — hydrogen embrittlement, and size growth against an m6 tolerance — that a soft part would never raise. Both are covered next in and .

The DIN 6325 footer: Werkstoff (material) — steel, minimum 600 N/mm² · Ausführung (condition) — gehärtet (hardened), Härte (hardness) 60 ± 2 HRC.

Topic T5 · Surface Treatment

Zinc Plating with Cr3 Passivate

The “-Z” in the part number calls out this finish. The item description reads “ZN” and the extended description reads “ZINC (Cr3)”.

Requirement

Zinc plated, with a trivalent chromate (Cr3) conversion coating — ZINC (Cr3).

Typical Call-Out

Electrodeposited zinc with a clear trivalent (Cr3) conversion, per ASTM F1941, which the SBS Finish Guide cites for zinc finishes.The guide lists clear trivalent codes Fe/Zn 3AN, 5AN and 8AN (3, 5 and 8 µm). This item’s page does not say which one applies.

Item H2 as received: the bright, slightly blue-silver zinc (Cr3) finish.

Meaning

Zinc is a sacrificial coating: it corrodes first, protecting the steel underneath. The Cr3 layer on top slows the zinc’s own corrosion and gives the clear, slightly blue look. It is a thin barrier: in the SBS Finish Guide, 5 µm clear trivalent zinc reaches white rust in about 8 hours of salt spray, and a sealer top coat extends that to 96 hours.

What Zinc (Cr3) Actually Is
  • A two-step finish: the pin is first electroplated with a thin layer of zinc, then dipped in a trivalent chromate solution that forms a clear conversion film on the zinc.
  • Cr3 means trivalent chromium (Cr3+). It replaces the older hexavalent (Cr6+) chromates that RoHS and REACH restrict — which is why the item page shows RoHS and REACH as compliant.
  • Unlike a conversion-only finish such as black oxide, zinc is a plated layer, typically 5–8 µm thick per surface. It adds size to the part.
  • Good general protection against shop and warehouse humidity at low cost — the usual reason a hardened pin is offered with a zinc finish.
Plain vs. Zinc (Cr3)
What the zinc finish looks like on this exact part (reference photo).

What Changes — and What Doesn’t

  1. Plain (unplated): bare dark steel that starts to rust quickly in humid air.
  2. Zinc (Cr3): bright, clear-blue silver, with the zinc taking the corrosion instead of the steel.
  3. Changed: the diameter grows by the thickness of the plating — see .

The Catch: Zinc on Hardened Steel

Hydrogen Embrittlement Key Risk

Electroplating a 60 HRC part is a recognized hydrogen-embrittlement risk. Plating standards call for baking hardened parts after plating, and some steer very hard parts toward non-electrolytic coatings instead.

How Hydrogen Embrittlement Happens

  1. Plating lets hydrogen in. Acid cleaning and the electroplating bath release hydrogen atoms, and some of them enter the surface of the steel.
  2. Hard steel traps it. The harder the steel, the less able it is to tolerate that hydrogen. The usual rule of thumb is concern above roughly 32–39 HRC, depending on the standard. This pin is at 60.
  3. Stress can crack it. Under load, a part carrying trapped hydrogen can crack suddenly, sometimes hours or days after plating, with no warning stretch.

The Standard Safeguard

A post-plate bake, typically around 200 °C for several hours and started soon after plating, drives the hydrogen back out of the steel.

What to Ask the Supplier

The item page does not state the bake or the plating thickness. Confirm both from the supplier’s certification before promising this pin for a high-load or safety-critical job. Dowels work in shear, not tension, which lowers the risk — it does not remove it.

Plating also changes the pin’s size, and for a precision dowel that matters. See .

Topic T6 · Precision Fit

The m6 Tolerance: An 8-Micron Window

The “m6” in the description is what makes this a dowel pin and not just a piece of rod: its diameter is held to a tight band so it locates parts the same way every time.

Requirement

Diameter 4 mm, tolerance zone m6: Min 4.004 / Max 4.012 mm (SBS Inspection Report, feature 5, checked with a micrometer).

Meaning

On a 4 mm size, m6 means +4 to +12 µm over nominal. That is a window only 8 µm (0.008 mm) wide — roughly a ninth of the width of a human hair.

How It Fits a Standard Hole

Mating hole shown as H7, the common reaming tolerance for dowel holes (shown for illustration; your drawing sets the hole). Both zones follow the ISO 286 limits for sizes from 3 to 6 mm.

A Transition Fit

H7 hole with an m6 pin is a transition fit: from 0.008 mm of clearance to 0.012 mm of interference. The pin seats snugly and locates repeatably, usually with a light tap or press, and still comes back out.

Why Not Looser?

Any clearance lets two parts shift when they are reassembled. The pin’s only job is to prevent that, so the diameter is the one dimension that has to be right.

Plating Eats the Window

Zinc Adds Size

A typical zinc layer is 5–8 µm on every surface, so the diameter grows by 10–16 µm — more than the whole 8 µm m6 window.

So It Is Controlled on the Finished Pin

The 4.004–4.012 mm limits on the inspection report apply to the finished .4R28MHD-Z, so the plating allowance has to be built into how the pin is ground before it is plated.

Diameter vs. Length

Diameter — Tight

Micrometer check: 4.004 to 4.012 mm, a total window of 0.008 mm.

Length — Loose

Caliper check: 27.63 to 28.37 mm, a window of 0.74 mm (±0.37). A dowel locates by its diameter, not its length, so length can be generous.

Reference

Glossary

Every code, acronym, and standard used in this module, defined in plain language. Tap a term’s “jump” button to see it in context.

ASTM F1941 / ISO 4042

Common standards for electroplated coatings on fasteners, including zinc and the rules for relieving hydrogen from hard parts. The SBS Finish Guide cites ASTM F1941 for zinc finishes; the item page does not say which code applies.

Chamfer

A small angled bevel at the end of a pin or shaft. DIN 6325 pins are chamfered and rounded at both ends so they start easily into a hole.

Cr3 (Trivalent Chromate)

A clear conversion film made with trivalent chromium (Cr3+) that is applied over zinc plating. It replaces the older hexavalent chromates restricted by RoHS and REACH.

DIN 6325 (ISO 8734)

The German standard, dated October 1971, for hardened parallel pins with an m6 tolerance. ISO 8734 (1997) is listed as its alternate in the SBS Standards Library.

Dowel Pin

A short, headless cylindrical pin pressed into holes in two parts to line them up precisely and carry shear load. It locates; it does not clamp.

HRC (Rockwell C)

A hardness scale for hardened steel. This pin is specified at 60 ± 2 HRC, far harder than a typical screw.

Hydrogen Embrittlement

Cracking of hard steel caused by hydrogen absorbed during plating. It is managed by baking the parts after plating.

m6 (Tolerance Zone)

An ISO tolerance zone for shafts. On a 4 mm diameter it means +4 to +12 µm over nominal, giving the 4.004–4.012 mm window.

PROP 65

A California law requiring a warning label on products containing certain chemicals above a set threshold. “Compliant” here means the part doesn’t trigger that warning.

PPAP

Production Part Approval Process — the documentation package a supplier submits to prove its process can reliably make a part to print. The report for this item lists the PPAP level as N/A.

REACH

A European Union regulation restricting hazardous chemicals in manufactured goods — a separate compliance check from RoHS, covering a broader list of substances.

RoHS

Restriction of Hazardous Substances — an EU rule limiting materials like lead, mercury and hexavalent chromium in manufactured parts.

Sacrificial Coating

A coating, such as zinc on steel, that corrodes first so the metal underneath doesn’t.

Track Lots

An ERP setting that records each received lot separately, so a pin can be traced back to its lot.

Transition Fit

A fit that can land anywhere from a small clearance to a small interference, depending on where each part falls in its tolerance. H7 hole with m6 pin is a transition fit.
